summary.text: A polar climate, letter E in the Köppen system, is one where every month averages below 10 °C, so there is no warm summer.
It comes in two types: tundra (ET), with at least one month above 0 °C, and ice cap (EF), with no month above 0 °C.
Köppen tied the 10 °C warmest-month line to tree lines, since places colder than that cannot support forests.

items.prompt: A remote island's warmest month averages 4 °C and its coldest −15 °C. Which climate type is it?

options.label: Ice cap climate
Tundra climate
Cold desert climate
Not polar, since it has a summer

items.explain: All months are below 10 °C, so it is polar; at least one month is above 0 °C, which makes it tundra rather than ice cap.

items.prompt: In a place where no month ever averages above 0 °C, what happens to snow and ice over time?

options.label: It melts away each short summer
It turns into tundra grassland
It builds up until it flows elsewhere
It blows away and leaves bare rock

items.explain: In an ice cap climate no plants grow and ice gradually accumulates until it flows or slides elsewhere.

items.prompt: The North Pole sits on ice over the Arctic Ocean. Why is it not the coldest spot in the Northern Hemisphere in winter?

options.label: The ocean water beneath stays relatively warm
It gets sunlight all through the winter
Warm winds from the tropics reach it daily
Its thick ice gives off heat as it forms

items.explain: Arctic ocean water can never fall below −2 °C, and this relatively warm water keeps the North Pole from being the hemisphere's coldest place.

items.prompt: Antarctica is technically classed as a desert. Why does so little precipitation reach most of it?

options.label: Sea ice soaks up all the rain offshore
Its high mountains block the summer sun
The air is too warm for snow to form
Weather fronts rarely reach far inland

items.explain: Antarctica averages about 166 mm of precipitation a year because weather fronts rarely penetrate far into the continent.

items.prompt: A high mountain far from the poles has no month averaging 10 °C. What is this climate called?

options.label: Subtropical climate
Maritime climate
Alpine climate
Rain shadow climate

items.explain: When the cold comes from elevation rather than latitude, the climate is referred to as alpine, and it can mimic tundra or ice cap.

items.prompt: Using Köppen's rule, a valley's warmest month averages 8 °C. Could a forest grow there?

options.label: Yes, if the winters are mild enough
No, it is below the tree line threshold
Yes, but only of coniferous trees
Only if the valley gets heavy rain

items.explain: Köppen found that places whose warmest month averages below 10 °C cannot support forests.

beats.hook: One number, the average of the warmest month, decides whether a place can grow a forest at all.

paragraphs.heading: What a polar climate is
paragraphs.text: A polar climate is one with no warm summer, though its winters can differ from place to place. Every month averages below 10 °C. In the Köppen climate classification it is marked with the letter E. Summers are cool and winters very cold, or there is no real summer at all, which leaves treeless tundra, glaciers or a lasting layer of ice. Together these regions cover more than 20% of Earth's area.

paragraphs.heading: Tundra and ice cap
paragraphs.text: There are two types. Tundra, coded ET, has at least one month averaging above 0 °C, while ice cap, coded EF, has none. In tundra not even conifers can grow, but specialised plants such as the arctic poppy can. In an ice cap climate no plants grow at all, and ice slowly builds up until it flows or slides somewhere else.

paragraphs.heading: Where they are
paragraphs.text: Most polar regions lie near the poles, where winter days are very short and summer days very long, sometimes for a whole season or more. Antarctica is the only continent where the ice cap type dominates, and nearly all of Greenland has it too, apart from coastal strips that have tundra. Tundra covers the far north of Eurasia, much of northern Siberia, northern Iceland, and large parts of northern Canada and Alaska. Many high mountain summits are polar as well; when the cold comes from height rather than latitude, it is called an alpine climate.

paragraphs.heading: Why the Arctic is milder
paragraphs.text: The Arctic is an ocean almost ringed by land such as Russia and Canada. Its seawater can never drop below −2 °C, so it softens the climate around it. In winter this comparatively warm water, even under the ice pack, stops the North Pole from being the coldest spot in the Northern Hemisphere, and it helps explain why Antarctica is so much colder. Antarctica has the coldest climate on Earth, with −89.2 °C measured at Vostok Station in 1983. It is also so dry that it counts as a polar desert, averaging 166 mm of precipitation a year, since weather fronts seldom reach far inland.

paragraphs.heading: Drawing the line with trees
paragraphs.text: Climatologist Wladimir Köppen linked the Arctic and Antarctic tree lines to a summer temperature of 10 °C: where the warmest month averages below that, forests cannot grow. Otto Nordenskjöld argued that winter matters too, with the formula W = 9 − 0.1 C, where W is the warmest month's average and C the coldest month's, both in °C. So a place whose coldest month averages −20 °C needs a warmest month of at least 11 °C for trees to survive, since 9 − 0.1(−20) = 11.
